slides.title: The Outbreak of War
body: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was the spark that ignited the powder keg of European tensions. In the streets of Sarajevo, Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Serbian nationalist, fired the shots that would echo across a century.

The political landscape of 1914 was defined by a complex web of mutual defence treaties. When Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, the gears of the alliance system began to turn with terrifying mechanical precision.

By August, the great powers were locked in a conflict that few expected to last more than a few months. The Schlieffen Plan — Germany's strategy to knock France out quickly by invading through neutral Belgium — ultimately drew Great Britain into the fray.

pullQuote.text: The lights are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our lifetime.

note.title: Archivist's Note
note.text: Princip belonged to 'The Black Hand', a secret military society. His success was largely accidental; the motorcade had taken a wrong turn and stalled right in front of him.

sections.heading: The Parapet
sections.body: The front wall, reinforced with sandbags and timber to protect against direct rifle fire and shrapnel.

sections.heading: Fire Step
sections.body: A raised ledge that let soldiers stand high enough to see over the parapet and fire during an attack.

sections.heading: Duckboards
sections.body: Wooden slats laid at the bottom of the trench to provide a dry walkway above the standing water and mud.

sections.heading: The Parados
sections.body: The rear wall, designed to protect soldiers from the concussive blast of shells falling behind the lines.

note.label: Archival Note
note.text: Trenches were never built in straight lines. A zig-zag or 'crenellated' pattern stopped a single shell or raider from clearing the whole length of the trench.

slides.title: The Western Front
slides.subtitle: Visualising the static 475-mile line of trenches that stretched from the Swiss border to the North Sea, defining the brutal stalemate of World War I.

note.label: Archival Note
note.quote: The line never moved more than a few miles in either direction for three years. It was a scar across the face of Europe.
note.name: Capt. Silas Thorne

footnotes.title: Trench Depth
footnotes.body: Typically 12 feet deep, constructed in a zig-zag pattern to minimise blast impacts.

footnotes.title: No Man's Land
footnotes.body: The deadly territory between opposing lines, often ranging from 50 to 250 yards wide.

footnotes.title: Logistic Network
footnotes.body: Behind the front lay millions of miles of telephone wire and secondary supply trenches.

slides.title: Video: The First Tanks
slides.body: In September 1916, during the Battle of the Somme, the British army unveiled a secret weapon that would change the face of warfare forever. The Mark I tank marked the first time armoured, motorised vehicles were used in combat, designed to break the bloody stalemate of trench warfare.
slides.quote: The monster approached... it passed over the trenches like a giant beetle, impervious to machine gun fire. — Archival Field Report, 1916.

slides.title: Knowledge Check: Trench Warfare
slides.question: Which breakthrough technology is most credited with finally ending the static stalemate of trench warfare?

feedback.correctText: Correct. The introduction of the tank allowed Allied forces to cross barbed wire and trenches that had previously pinned down infantry for years.
feedback.incorrectText: Incorrect. Consider the limitations of traditional mobility against entrenched machine gun nests. Try again.

artifact.caption: A steel beast designed to bridge the chasm of No Man's Land.

note.title: Archivist's Note
note.text: Tanks were first developed by the British Navy — hence the term 'Landships' — under the cover of a 'water tank' production project to maintain secrecy.
